keptItems.summaryEvidence: Weak scholarship was once easy to spot at a glance: The signs included bad writing, a lack of relevant citations, and little engagement with previous scholarship, such as a paper that promised a “novel” conceptual framework without acknowledging the many other papers making similar claims. keptItems.title: Israel’s Latest Last Chance to Save Itself
keptItems.summaryEvidence: I live on the same street in north Tel Aviv as Gali Baharav-Miara, Israel’s attorney general. Occasionally I see her walking through the neighborhood, a bodyguard following 20 feet behind. Her home is guarded around the clock. To the government and its supporters, she is an unelected official obstructing the elected right’s ability to govern. To liberal Israelis, she is one of the last institutional barriers between democracy and unchecked political power. The national argument plays itself out beneath my window. On Saturday nights, right-wing protesters gather outside her home, shouting, honking their horns, and demanding her dismissal. I’ve seen Mordechai David here, a right-wing activist who has become notorious for confronting prominent government opponents while filming them on his phone. On Friday afternoons, Baharav-Miara’s supporters take their place, wearing Gali, Guardian of Israel T-shirts and holding signs urging her to stay strong. Then everyone goes home. The street becomes quiet. The cafés open in the morning and we drink our coffee. Israelis have been predicting the end of Israel for as long as I can remember. In my liberal, secular circles, almost every election has been described as the decisive one, the last opportunity to save the country. If Menachem Begin wins, Israel is finished. If Ariel Sharon wins, Israel is finished. If Benjamin Netanyahu returns—again—Israel is finished. Friends announce that this time they really will leave. Yet when the results arrive, and despair descends, the following morning most wake up, drink their coffee, and go to work.

keptItems.title: Just Noting That Your Candy Corn Is Made of Bug Secretions
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Here’s a tip if you ever want to ruin a Halloween party. Seek out the most squeamish-seeming adult or child you can find in the act of consuming candy corn. Then tell them they just filled their mouth with bug secretions. If this fact alarms you—or if you’re an inveterate hater of candy corn and thus think that you have been spared—I regret to inform you that by eating many classic Halloween candies, you are, to some extent, eating bugs. More precisely, you are eating a bug by-product that is in many cases listed on the package as “confectioner’s glaze.” This glaze is used on jelly beans, Milk Duds, Junior Mints, Whoppers, Lemonheads, and Sugar Babies, to name a few. This sounds innocent enough, until you understand that the glaze is shellac—a shiny, moisture-blocking resin that’s the product of lac bugs’ lifelong work. As the female lac bug pierces a tree with her needlelike mouthparts and sucks the sap out, she secretes a goo, also called lac, from a gland on her abdomen to form a cocoon of sorts. (Male lac bugs don’t do much besides mate and die after about four days.) Inside her lac coating—which hardens on contact with the air much like, well, a candy shell—she spends her life feeding and laying eggs, safe from predators. If all goes well, she completes her life cycle and dies in her resinous home. The amount of resin produced by each insect is virtually microscopic, but over time, enough of the bugs cluster on one branch to make an amount worth pouring over a batch of Raisinets. keptItems.summaryEvidence: All Halloween candy is the same now. Nothing stands out, apart from the quantity of candy dumped out on the floor back home. Every house seems to buy a variety bag of seemingly random candy, and consequently every stop metes out a little more of the same treats as the previous one did or the next one will.
